1	# Performance baseline — all datasources
2	
3	> Captured **2026-07-10** against live warehouses. It measures, per datasource,
4	> where DataQ's run path stops scaling and *how it fails* when it does.
5	
6	## TL;DR
7	
8	| Datasource | Execution model | Verified scale | Ceiling on a 2 Gi worker | Failure mode past ceiling |
9	|---|---|---|---|---|
10	| **Snowflake** | SQL pushdown | **200M rows** (50M / 100M / 200M all green) | none found — worker memory flat | n/a |
11	| **Flat file CSV** (ADLS) | full load into worker pandas | 2M rows (~121 MB CSV) | **2M → 5M** | prefork child SIGKILL |
12	| **Flat file Parquet** (ADLS) | full load into worker pandas | 5M rows (~131 MB parquet) | **5M → 10M** | 5M+: child SIGKILL; 10M killed the whole container |
13	| **Unity Catalog** | full load via SQL-warehouse `read_sql_table` | 1M rows | **1M → 2M** | child SIGKILL |
14	| **Apache Iceberg** (native, ADR 0030) | full snapshot via `pyiceberg` → Arrow | 2M rows | **2M → 5M** | worker replica OOM-killed + recreated |
15	| **AWS S3** | same code as ADLS (`flatfile.py` is shared) | not run live (no S3 credentials remain) | expect ≡ ADLS | ≡ ADLS |
16	
17	Two sentences of conclusion:
18	
19	1. **Pushdown is a different regime, not a faster version of the same one.** At
20	   200M rows Snowflake's wall time is 16.2s (vs 12.1s at 50M) and the worker
21	   never moves off its ~930 MiB baseline; every full-load runner dies between
22	   1M and 10M rows depending on format.
23	2. **Past the ceiling, today's failure is silent** — the OOM-killed run sits in
24	   `running` for up to 60 minutes until the stuck-run reaper (#309) fails it,
25	   with no memory-attributed reason ([#755](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/755)).
26	   #595's size-probe + hard-cap ("refuse with `error`, don't OOM") is the fix.
27	
28	## Environment & method
29	
30	| | |
31	|---|---|
32	| App code | `main`, during v1.1 development |
33	| Measurement rig | docker-compose stack pinned to **production parity**: worker at 1 CPU / 2 GiB / `celery --concurrency=4` (matched to the deployed worker), driven through the real REST API |
34	| Iceberg leg | run against the deployed stack (the native catalog wasn't reachable from the local rig) — wall via REST, worker memory via the platform metric |
35	| Worker memory sampling | `docker stats` at 1 Hz (local); 1-min max metric (prod) |
36	| Checks per rung | 5 expectations (not-null ×2, between ×2, unique ×1) + volume & freshness monitors where the type supports them (SQL/UC/Iceberg — flat files reject monitor kinds by design) |
37	| Data shape | 6-col order-lines (`line_id`, `order_id`, `sku_id`, `qty`, `unit_price`, `line_ts`) — same shape as #587 |
38	
39	Data generation (all regenerable in seconds — nothing needs to be archived):
40	
41	- **Snowflake**: `CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT SEQ8(), UNIFORM(…), … FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 200000000))`
42	  — 50M in 10.6s, 100M in 17s, 200M in 28.6s on XSMALL. The 50M table was kept; the 100M/200M tables were dropped after the run.
43	- **UC**: `CREATE TABLE <catalog>.perf.order_lines_1m AS SELECT … FROM range(1000000)` via the SQL Statements API (schema dropped after).
44	- **Flat files**: numpy → CSV + Parquet at 1/2/5/10M rows, uploaded to `landing/perf/` (deleted after).
45	- **Iceberg**: 1M-row Arrow batches appended to a dedicated `perf.order_lines` namespace via `pyiceberg` (namespace dropped after the run).
46	
47	The whole campaign — including generating 350M+ Snowflake rows — burned
48	**~0.46 Snowflake credits** and roughly nothing anywhere else.
49	
50	## Snowflake — pushdown ramp
51	
52	| Rung | Wall (trigger → terminal) | Checks | Worker memory |
53	|---|---|---|---|
54	| 1.2M (#587, W1) | 12.2 s | 6 + volume, pass | < 50 MB delta |
55	| **50M** | **12.1 s** (repeat: 12.1 s) | 7/7 pass | baseline 923 → peak 926 MiB |
56	| **100M** | **16.2 s** | 7/7 pass | flat (≤ +2 MiB) |
57	| **200M** | **16.2 s** | 7/7 pass | flat (≤ +2 MiB) |
58	
59	Column profiler, 4 columns (`COUNT/nulls/distinct/min/max/top-10`):
60	
61	| Table | Cold | Warm repeat |
62	|---|---|---|
63	| 1.2M (#587) | 2.6 s | — |
64	| 50M | 15.7 s | 2.9 s |
65	| 200M | 24.6 s | 2.5 s |
66	
67	(The warm numbers are the Snowflake result cache doing the work — the app adds
68	~2.5s of fixed overhead.)
69	
70	Wall time is dominated by GX orchestration + connection setup exactly as #587
71	predicted: ~167× more rows (1.2M → 200M) bought ~4s of extra wall. Cost scales
72	with the *warehouse*, not the worker — the 2 Gi replica never noticed 200M rows.
73	
74	## Full-load runners — ramp to failure
75	
76	All numbers from the prod-parity rig except Iceberg (deployed stack). "Fresh" =
77	freshly restarted worker (baseline ~750–870 MiB); "warm" = worker that had
78	already executed runs (see the creep finding below).
79	
80	| Rung | Status | Wall | Worker peak |
81	|---|---|---|---|
82	| CSV 1M (60 MB) | pass | 4.0 s | 1186 MiB |
83	| CSV 2M (121 MB), warm | **child OOM** | — | killed at 1671 MiB |
84	| CSV 2M, fresh | pass | 6.1 s | 1211 MiB |
85	| CSV 5M (304 MB), fresh | **child OOM** | — | killed at 1838 MiB |
86	| Parquet 1M (26 MB) | pass | 4.0 s | 1295 MiB |
87	| Parquet 2M (53 MB) | pass | 6.0 s | 1666 MiB |
88	| Parquet 5M (131 MB), warm | **child OOM** | — | killed at 1915 MiB |
89	| Parquet 5M, fresh | pass | 8.1 s | 1508 MiB |
90	| Parquet 10M (263 MB), fresh | **container killed** | — | worker replica restarted mid-run |
91	| UC 1M | pass | 30.3 s | 1681 MiB |
92	| UC 2M | **child OOM** | — | killed seconds in |
93	| Iceberg 1M (deployed) | pass | 6.8 s | 1218 MiB (platform metric) |
94	| Iceberg 2M (deployed) | pass | 12.5 s | 1408 MiB |
95	| Iceberg 5M (deployed) | **container killed** | — | worker replica OOM-killed + recreated |
96	
97	Reading the table:
98	
99	- **Format matters ~2–4×**: parquet's ceiling is a rung above CSV's for the same
100	  row count (Arrow-backed read, no text parse blow-up).
101	- **UC is the heaviest per row** — `pd.read_sql_table` over the SQL warehouse
102	  spent ~925 MiB on 1M rows; it also pays a ~20s warehouse round-trip, so it's
103	  the slowest *and* the hungriest path.
104	- **Iceberg materialises the whole current snapshot** (`scan().to_arrow()`);
105	  its monitors (volume = `scan().count()`, freshness = single-column scan) stayed
106	  cheap and passed at every size tested.
107	
108	## Known limitations at the ceiling
109	
110	Two performance characteristics of the full-load path, both tracked for the
111	scale-aware execution work ([#595](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/595)):
112	
113	1. **An out-of-memory run is not reported promptly.** When a full-load run
114	   exceeds worker memory the worker process is killed; the run currently stays
115	   `running` until the stuck-run reaper fails it (default threshold 60 min),
116	   with no memory-attributed reason. Tracked in
117	   [#755](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/755) — the fix maps the
118	   worker loss straight to a run `error`, ahead of the #595 size-cap guardrail.
119	2. **The effective ceiling degrades with worker uptime.** The prefork worker's
120	   memory baseline creeps run-over-run (measured start-of-run: 956 → 1188 → 1666
121	   MiB across three flat-file runs) because children don't release pandas
122	   allocations — so a file that passes on a freshly-started worker can OOM on a
123	   long-lived one. Recycling children per N runs removes the creep (folded into
124	   #755).
125	
126	Two non-performance defects were also found and filed while measuring
127	([#753](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/753),
128	[#754](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/754)); see the tracker.
129	
130	## What this means for #595
131	
132	- The guardrail should be a **size probe + configurable hard cap** *before*
133	  materialising (refuse with a clean `error`), plus immediate `WorkerLostError`
134	  → run-failure mapping as defence in depth. A static row cap is the wrong knob:
135	  the measured ceiling varies ~5× by format and degrades with worker uptime.
136	- Sampling/batching priorities by measured pain: **UC first** (lowest ceiling,
137	  pushable — monitors already push down; SQL-able expectation subsets should
138	  too), then CSV (worst expansion factor; per-file batching already exists in the
139	  flat-file runner seam), then Iceberg (snapshot scan → `row_filter`/limit
140	  pushdown in pyiceberg).
141	- Per-run overhead floor is unchanged from #587 (~10s Snowflake, ~4s flat-file,
142	  ~6s Iceberg-on-prod), so sampled runs will be *fast*, not just safe.
143	
144	---
145	
146	## v1.1 — scale-aware execution ([#595](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/595))
147	
148	> Captured **2026-08-13** while building the sampling + guardrail work. This
149	> section answers the issue's last acceptance criterion ("volume test vs the #587
150	> Snowflake baseline documented") and records the evidence the shipped defaults
151	> were chosen from.
152	
153	### Method (and what it does *not* prove)
154	
155	A 5M-row, 6-column order-lines dataset (the same shape as every rung above) was
156	written as both CSV (**249 MB**) and Parquet (**114 MB**), and the **real**
157	`FlatFileCheckRunner` was run against it with five expectations (not-null ×2,
158	between ×2, unique ×1) — the same suite this campaign used.
159	
160	The three object-store seams (`file_stat` / `download_bytes` / `read_range`) were
161	pointed at a local file, so the runner, the guardrail and the sampling readers all
162	execute for real and only the network is stood in for. Peak memory is the child
163	process's own `ru_maxrss`.
164	
165	**What this does not measure:** egress, warehouse behaviour, or the Unity Catalog
166	leg — `TABLESAMPLE (x PERCENT)` is a Databricks-side fact and, per the #953 rule,
167	only a live run counts as evidence for it. The UC numbers below are therefore
168	absent rather than estimated.
169	
170	The **floor** — interpreter + GX + pyarrow, measured on the refused case, which
171	loads nothing — is **329 MiB**. Deltas below are over that floor, because it is
172	the part sampling cannot remove.
173	
174	### Results — 5M rows, five expectations
175	
176	| Object | Mode | Outcome | Wall | Peak RSS | Δ over floor |
177	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
178	| CSV 249 MB | full read, cap **off** | 5/5 pass | 4.26 s | **2,210 MiB** | +1,881 |
179	| CSV 249 MB | full read, cap **on** | **refused** — `ScanTooLargeError` | **0.00 s** | 329 MiB | +0 |
180	| CSV 249 MB | `head`, 100k rows | 5/5 pass, `sampled: true` | 0.15 s | **411 MiB** | +82 |
181	| CSV 249 MB | `random`, 100k rows | 5/5 pass, `sampled: true` | 1.98 s | **550 MiB** | +221 |
182	| Parquet 114 MB | full read, cap off | 5/5 pass | 2.11 s | 1,290 MiB | +961 |
183	| Parquet 114 MB | full read, cap on | 5/5 pass (under the cap) | 2.07 s | 1,278 MiB | +949 |
184	| Parquet 114 MB | `head`, 100k rows | 5/5 pass, `sampled: true` | 0.10 s | **405 MiB** | +76 |
185	| Parquet 114 MB | `random`, 100k rows | 5/5 pass, `sampled: true` | 0.18 s | **468 MiB** | +139 |
186	
187	Reading the table:
188	
189	1. **Without the cap, a 249 MB CSV needs 2.2 GiB.** That is over the deployed 2 GiB
190	   worker on its own, before the ~0.9 GiB baseline it already carries — i.e. the
191	   #755 SIGKILL, reproduced.
192	2. **With the cap, it is refused in 0.00 s** with a message naming the file, both
193	   numbers and the knob — instead of a dead child and a run stuck `running` for
194	   60 minutes with no memory-attributed reason.
195	3. **With sampling, the same five checks run under half a gigabyte**: 23× less
196	   memory delta and 28× less wall time for CSV `head`. `random` costs more than
197	   `head` because it has to learn the population size first (a streamed CSV scan;
198	   for Parquet that is a footer read, which is why the Parquet `random` case is
199	   nearly as cheap as `head`).
200	4. **Sampled-ness is recorded, and the record is honest about what it knows.**
201	   `head` reports `total_rows: null` — it stopped reading rather than pay for a
202	   count — while `random` reports `total_rows: 5000000`, because it needed the
203	   population size anyway.
204	
205	### Why the defaults are what they are
206	
207	`RUN_MAX_SCAN_BYTES = 128 MiB` and `RUN_MAX_SCAN_ROWS = 1,500,000`.
208	
209	The **first draft was 256 MiB and was wrong**, which is the useful part of this
210	measurement: the 249 MB CSV passes a 256 MiB cap and *still* peaks at 2,210 MiB.
211	A cap that admits the case it exists to prevent is a guardrail that does not
212	guard. At the measured expansion (~8× object bytes for CSV, ~9× for Parquet),
213	128 MiB puts a full read at roughly 1.2–1.3 GiB, which fits the deployed worker
214	with its baseline. It also lands exactly on the pass/fail boundary above: it
215	admits every rung measured to pass (121 MB CSV, 131 MB Parquet) and refuses every
216	rung measured to die (263 MB Parquet, 304 MB CSV).
217	
218	The Parquet row of the table is the honest edge case: at 114 MB it is *legally*
219	under the cap and still peaks at 1,278 MiB. That is the boundary, not a miss —
220	the next rung up (10M rows, ~228 MB) is refused. A deployment on a smaller worker
221	should lower the cap; a deployment on a larger one can raise it, and the message
222	says so.
223	
224	`RUN_MAX_SCAN_ROWS` keeps the UC datum: 1M passed at 1,681 MiB, 2M OOM-killed
225	the child, so 1.5M sits between them. It is a **row** cap rather than a byte one
226	because a warehouse `COUNT(*)` is exact and free, where a CSV's row count would
227	cost the very scan being avoided.
228	
229	### Comparison with the #587 Snowflake baseline
230	
231	The point of the comparison is that these are still two different regimes, and
232	sampling narrows the gap without closing it:
233	
234	| | Snowflake (pushdown) | Flat file, full read | Flat file, sampled |
235	|---|---|---|---|
236	| Rows the worker holds | none | all of them | the sample |
237	| 5M rows, peak worker RSS | flat (≤ +2 MiB at 200M) | 1,290–2,210 MiB | 405–550 MiB |
238	| Scales with | the warehouse | the dataset | the sample |
239	| Answer is | complete | complete | **a sample — and says so** |
240	
241	Pushdown remains strictly better where it is available, which is why
242	`SAMPLING_CAPABLE_TYPES` excludes Snowflake outright rather than offering a knob
243	that would stamp "sampled" on a result that was not.
244	
245	### Still open after this work
246	
247	- **Unity Catalog needs a live run.** The pushdown SQL is DataQ's own
248	  construction and is unit-pinned, but `TABLESAMPLE (x PERCENT) REPEATABLE (seed)`
249	  behaviour is a Databricks fact — #953's rule says only a live run is evidence.
250	- **Iceberg has neither a cap nor sampling**
251	  ([#1328](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1328)). It is the third
252	  runner that materialises a whole dataset, so #755 stays open there. The probe is
253	  cheap (`scan().count()` is snapshot metadata); what it needs first is its **own
254	  measurement** — Iceberg passed at 2M rows where UC died, so inheriting
255	  `RUN_MAX_SCAN_ROWS`'s 1.5M would refuse a rung measured to work.
256	- **Comparison sources cannot sample**
257	  ([#1331](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1331)) — refused at save
258	  time rather than ignored. It needs *coherent* key-set sampling: two independent
259	  draws from two 5M-row sides would share almost no keys and report everything as
260	  a mismatch, which is worse than refusing.
261	- **Column projection for flat-file monitors.** A column-freshness monitor still
262	  reads every column to compute one `MAX`. Parquet could project a single column
263	  off its footer, which would remove most of the remaining monitor-path memory.
264	- **Efficiency and reuse batches**
265	  ([#1329](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1329),
266	  [#1330](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1330)) — the sampled CSV
267	  `random` path reads the object twice, and the count and take construct their CSV
268	  streams separately (consistent today by coincidence, not construction).
269	- **Incremental / delta-only validation** stays out of scope by design (#595):
270	  sampling bounds *how much* is read, not *which part is new*. Note for whoever
271	  builds it — a watermark belongs on the run target beside `sampling`, and its
272	  result record should be the same shape as `sampling`, so the run-detail surface
273	  learns one vocabulary for "this verdict covers less than everything".
274	
275	---

**UC engine routing (as of #1532/#1533):**
- Custom SQL / `UnexpectedRowsExpectation` → always the Databricks-SQL batch (GX SqlAlchemy engine).
- Ordinary audited expectations (not-null, unique, between, in-set, length, regex, row-count) → **Databricks-SQL batch by default** now (since #1532/#1533), gated by `UC_SQL_PUSHDOWN` (default true) and only when no sample is declared and the target has valid identifiers.
- `expect_column_values_to_be_of_type` and any unaudited type → DataFrame (pandas) batch via `pd.read_sql_table`/`_query`, full-load into worker memory.
- Any check on a sampled suite target → forced to the DataFrame batch (sampling bypasses pushdown).
- Monitors (`freshness`/`volume`), `schema_drift`, `anomaly` → GX-free, direct SQLAlchemy aggregates.
- `comparison` → separate pandas-based engine, unrelated to GX/UC batches.

**GX Spark?** No — confirmed by grep across `backend/app` and dependency files: no `pyspark`, `SparkDFExecutionEngine`, or Spark GX datasource anywhere. UC uses only GX's Databricks-SQL (SQLAlchemy) engine and GX's pandas engine.

**On the perf test:** `docs/site/perf-baseline.md` (2026-07-10 + 2026-08-13 addenda) is the tracked baseline, and it's now stale specifically for UC — it measured the *old* all-DataFrame-load UC path (1M pass / 2M OOM), but #1532/#1533 just made ordinary expectations pushdown to SQL by default, which should change that profile substantially (most checks no longer materialize the table into worker memory at all). It's also the one leg the doc flagged as needing a live run (`TABLESAMPLE`/pushdown behavior is a Databricks fact per the #953 rule).

**Why not pushdown everywhere:** it's a deliberately audited allowlist, not a technical ceiling. `SQL_PUSHDOWN_EXPECTATION_TYPES` (unity_catalog.py:178-182) only contains 7 expectation types that have been **live-verified per #953** ("only a live run is evidence" for anything crossing a driver boundary — GX's SqlAlchemy metric translation per expectation type is exactly that kind of boundary). Widening it is "a deliberate edit, not something that happens by accident" (line 172) — each new type needs its own live-verification pass against Databricks before being trusted, since GX's SQL metric providers vary in maturity/dialect-correctness per expectation type. `expect_column_values_to_be_of_type` is excluded on principle, not audit-laziness: its authored `type_` values are pandas dtypes, but the SQL engine checks reflected SQLAlchemy types — pushing it down would silently flip what existing checks mean. Custom SQL is separate: it always needs SQL because `UnexpectedRowsExpectation` has no pandas metric provider at all, so that's not a choice, it's a hard requirement.

**Why no Spark:** DataQ's Databricks connection is a **SQL warehouse** (via `databricks-sql-connector`/SQLAlchemy), not a cluster — there's no Spark compute in the picture at all today. Using GX's `SparkDFExecutionEngine` would require standing up `pyspark`/`databricks-connect`, provisioning cluster compute (interactive or job cluster, a different cost/infra model than a SQL warehouse), and a second auth path. Given that the audited pushdown set already covers the common expectations via SQL (zero worker memory, scales with the warehouse), and everything else falls back to a *sampled/bounded* pandas frame (post-#595), there's been no case yet that's simultaneously (a) not SQL-pushable and (b) too large for sampled pandas — which is the only gap Spark would actually close. It'd be a real dependency + infra addition for a case that hasn't materialized.

Given that, want me to scope the perf test as: measure the *current* UC ramp (1M/2M/5M) now that the 7 audited types pushdown by default, to see whether the old ceiling (1M pass / 2M OOM) still applies to whatever's left on the pandas path — confirming pushdown actually moved the needle rather than assuming it did?
do we need to deploy the code in-order to get the pushdown perf result?

No — the perf-baseline methodology never tested against the deployed Azure/AWS containers. It ran a local docker-compose stack (worker pinned to prod-parity: 1 CPU/2 GiB/`celery --concurrency=4`) checked out at whatever commit, driven through the real REST API against a **live UC connection** (harness or prod Databricks). The code just needs to be on the checked-out branch/commit — `main` already has #1533 merged, so a local worker built from `main` exercises the real pushdown path.

We do need a live UC connection to run against (Databricks SQL warehouse + real table), same as before — that's the harness/prod-credential question, unrelated to deployment.

Why we are not using push down everywhere? - Is it delibared? if so what is the rational?  
And why there is no spark?
Do we need spark [will help to offload the compute from dataq for UC, as UC warehouse will anyway have a compute serverless or dedicated server]?

**1. Is the pushdown allowlist deliberate? Yes — it's an audit boundary, not a capability limit.**

The rationale, from [unity_catalog.py:178-182](backend/app/datasources/unity_catalog.py#L178-L182) and the #1532 work:

- **Each expectation type's SQL translation is GX's code, not ours, and it crosses a driver boundary.** GX compiles each expectation into SqlAlchemy metrics per dialect. Whether that compilation is *correct on Databricks* varies per expectation type — and per the #953 standing rule ("for anything crossing a driver boundary, only a live run is evidence"), each type gets pushed down only after being live-verified against a real Databricks warehouse. The 7 in `SQL_PUSHDOWN_EXPECTATION_TYPES` (not-null, unique, between, in-set, length, regex, row-count) are the audited set. Anything unaudited falls back to the pandas frame — a slower path that's *known* to work beats a faster path that's assumed to.
- **One type is excluded on semantics, not audit backlog:** `expect_column_values_to_be_of_type` — authored `type_` values are pandas dtypes (`int64`, `object`); the SQL engine compares reflected SQLAlchemy types. Pushing it down would silently change what every existing check means.
- **Sampled suites force the frame path** — a SQL batch runs against the whole table, which would make the result claim more coverage than the suite's declared sample.
- It's declared as data with a canary test, so widening it is a conscious per-type decision (audit → live-verify → add), not drift.

So the trajectory is "pushdown everywhere it's proven" — the allowlist is expected to grow, one live-verified type at a time.

**2 & 3. Why no Spark — and do we need it? No, because pushdown already achieves exactly the offload you're describing.**

Your premise is right: the UC warehouse has its own compute (serverless or dedicated), and DataQ shouldn't hold rows in its 2 GiB worker. But **SQL pushdown is precisely that offload** — the Databricks-SQL batch sends the check as SQL, the warehouse's compute (which *is* Spark under the hood — Photon/Spark executing your SQL) does all the scanning, and the worker gets back scalars. The Snowflake baseline shows what that regime looks like: 200M rows, worker memory flat at ≤+2 MiB. Post-#1532, UC's audited expectations are in that same regime.

Adding GX's `SparkDFExecutionEngine` would *not* add offload — it would add a second, worse way to reach the same compute:

- The current connection is a **SQL warehouse** via `databricks-sql-connector`. A SQL warehouse doesn't accept Spark DataFrame jobs — GX-Spark would need `databricks-connect`/Spark Connect against an **all-purpose cluster**: a different compute type, different (higher, always-on-ish) cost model, a second auth/connection surface per UC connection, plus a heavy `pyspark` dependency in the worker image.
- What it would buy is only the residual frame path: `to_be_of_type`, not-yet-audited types, and sampled suites. Those are already memory-bounded post-#595 (sampling caps + `RUN_MAX_SCAN_ROWS=1.5M` refuse-don't-OOM), and the cheaper fix for that residue is auditing more types into the pushdown set — not a new execution engine.

Spark would become worth revisiting only if a check class emerges that is (a) inexpressible in SQL and (b) too big to sample honestly — nothing in the current kind/type inventory is both. And note ADR 0036 already reserves the Databricks-native lane for **DQX** as UC's second engine (DLT/streaming), which is the more idiomatic Databricks answer than GX-Spark would be.

Want me to proceed with the UC pushdown perf run (local `main` stack, live UC connection via the harness)?

what are the real-world chances [even for enterprise scenarios] that we need spark?
And what is happening for UC custom sql?

**Real-world odds you'd need Spark: low — I'd put it under ~5% of enterprise UC deployments, and even those cases mostly point at DQX, not GX-Spark.**

Reasoning by scenario:

- **Scale alone never requires it.** DQ checks are overwhelmingly declarative predicates and aggregates — null/unique/range/set/regex/row-count/freshness/volume — all SQL-expressible, all executed by the warehouse's own compute (which is Spark/Photon anyway). Snowflake proved the regime: 200M rows, flat worker memory. There is no table size at which SQL pushdown stops working and Spark starts being necessary.
- **"We have cluster compute but no SQL warehouse"** — the one structurally real case. Some enterprises run jobs-only Databricks (no warehouse endpoint). But serverless SQL warehouses have made this shrinking and rare, and a warehouse for DQ probes is cheap since checks are short-lived queries.
- **Non-SQL-expressible logic at full-table scale** — ML-ish checks (fuzzy dedupe, entity resolution, learned anomaly models over raw rows). Genuinely exists in large enterprises, but it's a specialist tail; DataQ's anomaly kind already covers the common version (statistical baseline over `metric_value` scalars) with zero row movement. And a customer with that need on Databricks would reach for **DQX or a notebook job**, not expect their DQ monitoring tool to embed pyspark.
- **Streaming/DLT expectations** — real enterprise demand, and exactly why ADR 0036 reserves DQX as UC's second engine. GX is batch-only; GX-Spark wouldn't fix that either.

So the honest posture: the pressure Spark would relieve is already relieved by (a) growing the audited pushdown set and (b) the DQX lane. GX-Spark specifically has no constituency.

**UC custom SQL: it always executes on the warehouse, unconditionally.**

`is_custom_sql` routes it to the Databricks-SQL batch regardless of the `UC_SQL_PUSHDOWN` flag ([unity_catalog.py:517-520](backend/app/datasources/unity_catalog.py#L517-L520)) — not an optimization but a hard requirement: GX's `UnexpectedRowsExpectation` has only a SqlAlchemy metric provider, no pandas one, so it *cannot* run on the DataFrame batch. That's also the #1179 backstory: before the SQL batch existed, ADR 0019's UC custom SQL had never once worked (run or dry-run). Mechanically, GX builds and owns its own second engine via `add_databricks_sql` (separate from the runner's shared engine), the warehouse runs your query, and the worker only receives the unexpected-row output. Two caveats to know: on a **sampled** suite, custom SQL still runs against the *whole table* (a sample can't be threaded into arbitrary user SQL — deliberate, documented in the routing comments), and it stays SQL-batch even when `UC_SQL_PUSHDOWN=false` since the rollback flag only governs the ordinary-expectation routing.

import os
import time
import json
import urllib.request

HOST = os.environ["DATABRICKS_HOST"].rstrip("/")
TOKEN = os.environ["DATABRICKS_TOKEN"]
WAREHOUSE_ID = "b6403b6e3734f0ce"
CATALOG = "dataq_retail"


def run_sql(statement, wait_timeout="50s"):
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{HOST}/api/2.0/sql/statements",
        data=json.dumps(
            {
                "warehouse_id": WAREHOUSE_ID,
                "statement": statement,
                "wait_timeout": wait_timeout,
                "catalog": CATALOG,
            }
        ).encode(),
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        method="POST",
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:
        result = json.load(resp)

    statement_id = result["statement_id"]
    status = result["status"]["state"]
    while status in ("PENDING", "RUNNING"):
        time.sleep(2)
        poll_req = urllib.request.Request(
            f"{HOST}/api/2.0/sql/statements/{statement_id}",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"},
        )
        with urllib.request.urlopen(poll_req) as resp:
            result = json.load(resp)
        status = result["status"]["state"]

    if status != "SUCCEEDED":
        raise RuntimeError(f"statement failed: {json.dumps(result, indent=2)[:2000]}")
    return result


print("creating perf schema...")
run_sql(f"CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS {CATALOG}.perf")

for rows, name in [(1_000_000, "order_lines_1m"), (2_000_000, "order_lines_2m")]:
    print(f"creating {name} ({rows} rows)...")
    run_sql(f"DROP TABLE IF EXISTS {CATALOG}.perf.{name}")
    run_sql(
        f"""
        CREATE TABLE {CATALOG}.perf.{name} AS
        SELECT
          id AS line_id,
          CAST(id / 5 AS BIGINT) AS order_id,
          CAST(1 + (id % 500) AS BIGINT) AS sku_id,
          CAST(1 + (id % 20) AS INT) AS qty,
          CAST(5 + (id % 1000) / 10.0 AS DOUBLE) AS unit_price,
          TIMESTAMP'2026-01-01 00:00:00' + (id % 5000) * INTERVAL 1 MINUTE AS line_ts
        FROM range({rows}) AS t(id)
        """,
        wait_timeout="50s",
    )

print("verifying row counts...")
for name in ("order_lines_1m", "order_lines_2m"):
    res = run_sql(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {CATALOG}.perf.{name}")
    count = res["result"]["data_array"][0][0]
    print(f"  {name}: {count}")

print("done")

import os
import time
import json
import urllib.request

HOST = os.environ["DATABRICKS_HOST"].rstrip("/")
TOKEN = os.environ["DATABRICKS_TOKEN"]
WAREHOUSE_ID = "b6403b6e3734f0ce"
CATALOG = "dataq_retail"


def run_sql(statement, wait_timeout="50s"):
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{HOST}/api/2.0/sql/statements",
        data=json.dumps(
            {
                "warehouse_id": WAREHOUSE_ID,
                "statement": statement,
                "wait_timeout": wait_timeout,
                "catalog": CATALOG,
            }
        ).encode(),
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        method="POST",
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:
        result = json.load(resp)

    statement_id = result["statement_id"]
    status = result["status"]["state"]
    while status in ("PENDING", "RUNNING"):
        time.sleep(3)
        poll_req = urllib.request.Request(
            f"{HOST}/api/2.0/sql/statements/{statement_id}",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"},
        )
        with urllib.request.urlopen(poll_req) as resp:
            result = json.load(resp)
        status = result["status"]["state"]

    if status != "SUCCEEDED":
        raise RuntimeError(f"statement failed: {json.dumps(result, indent=2)[:2000]}")
    return result


rows, name = 50_000_000, "order_lines_50m"
print(f"creating {name} ({rows} rows)...")
run_sql(f"DROP TABLE IF EXISTS {CATALOG}.perf.{name}")
t0 = time.time()
run_sql(
    f"""
    CREATE TABLE {CATALOG}.perf.{name} AS
    SELECT
      id AS line_id,
      CAST(id / 5 AS BIGINT) AS order_id,
      CAST(1 + (id % 500) AS BIGINT) AS sku_id,
      CAST(1 + (id % 20) AS INT) AS qty,
      CAST(5 + (id % 1000) / 10.0 AS DOUBLE) AS unit_price,
      TIMESTAMP'2026-01-01 00:00:00' + (id % 5000) * INTERVAL 1 MINUTE AS line_ts
    FROM range({rows}) AS t(id)
    """,
    wait_timeout="50s",
)
print(f"create took {time.time() - t0:.1f}s")

## v1.2 — UC SQL pushdown for ordinary expectations ([#1532](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1532)/[#1533](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1533))

> Captured **2026-08-22**, live against the harness Databricks workspace. This
> closes the one gap the v1.1 section above left open ("Unity Catalog needs a
> live run") — it re-measures the UC leg now that the seven audited ordinary
> expectations (not-null, unique, between, in-set, length, regex, row-count)
> execute on the Databricks-SQL batch by default (`UC_SQL_PUSHDOWN=true`) instead
> of the full pandas-frame load the earlier baseline measured.

### Method

Same shape as every prior rung: a 6-col order-lines table (`line_id`, `order_id`,
`sku_id`, `qty`, `unit_price`, `line_ts`), created via
`CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT … FROM range(n)` on the harness's Databricks Free
Edition serverless SQL warehouse, run through the **real** `UnityCatalogCheckRunner`
via the prod-parity rig (worker capped 1 CPU / 2 GiB, `celery --concurrency=4`),
driven through the real REST API. Suite: the same 5 expectations as every other
rung (not-null ×2, between ×2, unique ×1) — all five are in the audited pushdown
allowlist. Worker memory sampled via `docker stats` at ~1 Hz; "wall" is
`started_at` → `finished_at` from the run record.

### Results

| Rows | Pushdown | Outcome | Wall | Worker peak | Δ over idle baseline |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1M | **off** (frame load, pre-#1532 behavior) | 5/5 pass | 11.1 s | **1,588 MiB** (1.551 GiB) | +824 MiB (over 764 MiB) |
| 1M | **on** (default) | 5/5 pass | 17.7 s | **935 MiB** | +15 MiB (over 920 MiB) |
| 2M | **off** | **refused** — `ScanTooLargeError`-class guardrail | 1.7 s | 791 MiB | +0 |
| 2M | **on** (default) | 5/5 pass | 16.6 s | **942 MiB** | +22 MiB (over 920 MiB) |
| 50M | **on** (default) | 5/5 pass | 20.2 s | **968 MiB** | +48 MiB (over 920 MiB) |

The 1M off/on pair is the clean comparison — same table, same suite, back-to-back
on freshly-restarted workers, only the `UC_SQL_PUSHDOWN` flag differs.

### Reading the table

1. **The old 1M→2M ceiling is gone for audited checks.** The v1.1 section above
   measured UC as the *worst* full-load runner: 1M passed at 1,681 MiB, 2M
   child-OOM'd within seconds. Pushed down, 2M now runs in the same ~940 MiB
   envelope as 1M — the table that used to kill the worker is now a non-event.
   50M rows (25× the old ceiling) still holds flat at 968 MiB, matching the
   Snowflake pushdown shape ("cost scales with the warehouse, not the worker")
   rather than UC's old full-load shape.

import os
import time
import json
import urllib.request

HOST = os.environ["DATABRICKS_HOST"].rstrip("/")
TOKEN = os.environ["DATABRICKS_TOKEN"]
WAREHOUSE_ID = "b6403b6e3734f0ce"
CATALOG = "dataq_retail"


def run_sql(statement, wait_timeout="50s"):
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{HOST}/api/2.0/sql/statements",
        data=json.dumps(
            {
                "warehouse_id": WAREHOUSE_ID,
                "statement": statement,
                "wait_timeout": wait_timeout,
                "catalog": CATALOG,
            }
        ).encode(),
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        method="POST",
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:
        result = json.load(resp)

    statement_id = result["statement_id"]
    status = result["status"]["state"]
    while status in ("PENDING", "RUNNING"):
        time.sleep(3)
        poll_req = urllib.request.Request(
            f"{HOST}/api/2.0/sql/statements/{statement_id}",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"},
        )
        with urllib.request.urlopen(poll_req) as resp:
            result = json.load(resp)
        status = result["status"]["state"]

    if status != "SUCCEEDED":
        raise RuntimeError(f"statement failed: {json.dumps(result, indent=2)[:2000]}")
    return result


run_sql("CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS dataq_retail.perf")

for rows, name in [(100_000_000, "order_lines_100m"), (200_000_000, "order_lines_200m")]:
    print(f"creating {name} ({rows} rows)...")
    run_sql(f"DROP TABLE IF EXISTS {CATALOG}.perf.{name}")
    t0 = time.time()
    run_sql(
        f"""
        CREATE TABLE {CATALOG}.perf.{name} AS
        SELECT
          id AS line_id,
          CAST(id / 5 AS BIGINT) AS order_id,
          CAST(1 + (id % 500) AS BIGINT) AS sku_id,
          CAST(1 + (id % 20) AS INT) AS qty,
          CAST(5 + (id % 1000) / 10.0 AS DOUBLE) AS unit_price,
          TIMESTAMP'2026-01-01 00:00:00' + (id % 5000) * INTERVAL 1 MINUTE AS line_ts
        FROM range({rows}) AS t(id)
        """,
        wait_timeout="50s",
    )
    print(f"  create took {time.time() - t0:.1f}s")

for name in ("order_lines_100m", "order_lines_200m"):
    res = run_sql(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {CATALOG}.perf.{name}")
    print(f"  {name}: {res['result']['data_array'][0][0]}")

print("done")

"""Guardrails for custom-SQL checks (ADR 0019).

A custom-SQL check is a GX ``UnexpectedRowsExpectation``: a normal
``kind='expectation'`` check with ``expectation_type='unexpected_rows_expectation'``
and ``config={'unexpected_rows_query': '<SQL with {batch}>'}``. It rides the
existing model / runner / result path unchanged — the only thing v1 adds is this
single guardrail, reused by every authoring path (check CRUD + suite import).

Two checks:

1. **Datasource gating** — custom-SQL is offered only for SQL-queryable
   datasources (Snowflake, Unity Catalog). Flat-file stores (ADLS / S3) are GX
   DataFrame assets, not SQL, so the query could never run there.
2. **Read-only, single statement** — the query must be a single ``SELECT`` /
   ``WITH`` statement with no DML/DDL/DCL. This is **best-effort, defence-in-depth,
   not a SQL firewall** (ADR 0019): the real boundary is the connection's
   least-privilege role. We strip string literals / quoted identifiers / comments
   before scanning so a literal ``'delete'`` or a column named ``"update"`` is not
   mistaken for a keyword, then require a read-only shape.

FastAPI-free like the sibling services: raises ``DataQError`` subclasses.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
import string
from typing import Any

from backend.app.core.errors import DataQError

# Trailing characters a single statement may end with (whitespace + a closing
# semicolon). Stripped with str.rstrip (linear) rather than a `[;\s]+$` regex,
# which is a polynomial-ReDoS sink on the user-provided query (CodeQL).
_TRAILING_CHARS = string.whitespace + ";"

# The GX expectation a custom-SQL check maps to (ADR 0019).
CUSTOM_SQL_EXPECTATION_TYPE = "unexpected_rows_expectation"
# The GX kwarg holding the user's query.
QUERY_KEY = "unexpected_rows_query"

# Datasources GX can run SQL against (ADR 0019). Flat files (adls_gen2 / s3) are
# DataFrame assets; orchestration types (adf / airflow) aren't datasources at all.
SQL_QUERYABLE_TYPES = frozenset({"snowflake", "unity_catalog"})
